> However, this introduces more complexity, [causes unexpected error](https://github.com/starship/starship/issues/590) and [slows down startup time](https://github.com/starship/starship/issues/1032) (because Starship are invoked **twice** during initialization, and in Fish `psub` will need to call `mktemp` and `rm`).

I wholeheartedly agree except I don't see init slowdowns as a big deal in the age of large shell frameworks people are using these days.


> You may argue it's for consistency, but the truth is, every shell _is_ different, so we should use the most _native_ approach if possible.

Technically speaking you are right but I'd argue that one of the selling points of Starship is more or less uniform and short initialization step across multiple shells further strengthening its image of a familiar bridge between different worlds. That is not really an argument pro or contra rather a philosophical observation. 🤷 

Maybe doing what you said minus bash is a step in the right direction. What I mean is to do a single pass for all other supported shells and keep 2 phase init (with eval) for bash exclusively. I understand that means going a long way in supporting legacy stuff but we could try at least. Plus we could possibly get rid of that full init flag altogether by the smart recursive calling of the same bash snippet that acts both as router and actual init itself? 💡
I think the biggest thing against changing this is that it would be a massive breaking change for the majority of starship users. This might be something we have to leave until v2.

> I think the biggest thing against changing this is that it would be a massive breaking change for the majority of starship users. This might be something we have to leave until v2.

This is a good point! We could, however, deprecate it first with printing warnings on init. 🤔

I left some additional notes on this topic in https://github.com/starship/starship/issues/5229, but leaving the TLDR here:

For `zsh`, one invocation can be dropped entirely. This PoC patch simply outputs the full initialisation script on the first execution and skips the second entirely.

```diff
diff --git a/src/init/mod.rs b/src/init/mod.rs
index f0b247c9..90399a18 100644
--- a/src/init/mod.rs
+++ b/src/init/mod.rs
@@ -153,10 +153,7 @@ pub fn init_stub(shell_name: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
             "#,
             starship.sprint_posix()?
         ),
-        "zsh" => print!(
-            r#"source <({} init zsh --print-full-init)"#,
-            starship.sprint_posix()?
-        ),
+        "zsh" => print_script(ZSH_INIT, &starship.sprint_posix()?),
         "fish" => print!(
             // Fish does process substitution with pipes and psub instead of bash syntax
             r#"source ({} init fish --print-full-init | psub)"#,
```

I built starship with the above patch and then using it directly worked fine by using `eval "$(/home/hugo/src/github.com/starship/starship/target/debug/starship init zsh)"`. This is backwards compatible and does not require any changes in the installation instructions (so honestly, it could be push without a major release).

Note that it would still be possible to update the installation instructions to `source <(starship init zsh)`; my patch work with both `source` and `eval`. I simply haven't tested which is more performant.

I left `init_main` untouched in this case, although technically it should never be executed for `zsh`, so I could drop the branch in the `match` for it entirely.

Shall I open a PR for this?

---

OTOH: The shell-specific way of doing this would be to install the initialisation script into `$fpath` and  then use `autoload -Uz starship-init;starship-init in `zshrc`. This is the simplest and also most performant approach, but makes the zsh setup process a bit of a snowflake and I don't expect you want to deal with this kind of thing upstream.

Sorry if this seems like a silly question, but why exactly do we have to invoke `starship init ...` with each shell startup at all?

I recently looked at the biggest slowdowns of my Zsh, and it turned out `starship` was the main culprit there (invoking an external binary costs about 30ms on my 2014 Macbook Pro).

IMHO calling an external binary should be done only if the builtin shell tools (functions, sourced scripts, ...) are really slower than the cost of calling a binary.
With that in mind, this is how I ended up initializing starship (this can be made less verbose of course):

```zsh
starship_cache_dir="$HOME/.cache/starship"
starship_script="$starship_cache_dir/init.zsh"

if [ ! -d "$starship_cache_dir" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$starship_cache_dir"
fi

if [ ! -f "$starship_script" ]; then
    starship init zsh --print-full-init > "$starship_script"
fi

source "$starship_script"
```

And here's a simple comparison measured with [hyperfine](https://github.com/sharkdp/hyperfine):
| Initialization | Startup time | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No starship initialization | 64ms | 0ms |
| Starship initialization with cached script | 78ms | + 14ms |
| Starship initialization with `eval "$(starship init zsh)"` | 107ms | + 43ms |

Measured as follows: `hyperfine --warmup 3 "zsh -l -i -c exit"`

@etienne-k Can you test if the slowdown is as substantial with 1.17.0? In includes [this improvement for zsh](https://github.com/starship/starship/pull/5322) which should trim down the startup cost (it executes `starship` just once rather than twice).

See also "possible solution 3" here if you want to work on more performance zsh-specific approaches.: https://github.com/starship/starship/issues/5229

> Sorry if this seems like a silly question, but why exactly do we have to invoke `starship init ...` with each shell startup at all?

The init-scripts has been evolving over time, and this ensures the current version is used and doesn't require any housekeeping.

> Can you test if the slowdown is as substantial with 1.17.0? 

1.17.0 has not been released yet.

I could try to build starship from source, but keep in mind most time gets lost when zsh needs to fork + exec starship. Removing an indirection should optimize this, but we're still left with an invocation of the starship binary, which is the main performance culprit.

@WhyNotHugo you're right, it seems like you had the idea before me, in "solution 3" in #5229.

> This would make starship less of a snowflake from the zsh perspective, but it would probably make zsh more of a snowflake from the starship perspective. I'm not sure you'd want to deal with the nuances of this upstream.

That said, I don't think the strategy of _generating once and sourcing_ makes zsh that much of a snowflake from the starship perspective. We do this for Nushell already.

Finally, if, for some reason, the one liner (with or without additional indirection) is wanted, it would be really nice if starship documented both the simple one-liner and the more performant version; an approach also followed by frameworks like [antidote](https://getantidote.github.io/install#ultra-high-performance-install).
That would allow user to choose what they want, and it would avoid propagating a "bad habbit" when [integrating starship in other systems](https://github.com/nix-community/home-manager/blob/master/modules/programs/starship.nix#L110).

@usagi-flow Feel free to experiment with the startup script. Something that can be installed into `$fpath` and loaded via zsh's `autoload` would likely be the best design for something zsh-specific and the lightest thing possible.
